summary: In Mata v. Avianca, attorneys submitted court materials relying on nonexistent judicial opinions generated by ChatGPT. The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York found that the respondents submitted fake opinions and continued to stand by them after their authenticity was questioned, and imposed sanctions including a US$5,000 penalty.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: In Mata v. Avianca, attorneys submitted court materials relying on nonexistent judicial opinions generated by ChatGPT. The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York found that the respondents submitted fake opinions and continued to stand by them after their authenticity was questioned, and imposed sanctions including a US$5,000 penalty. The primary opinion distinguishes Schwartz’s research, LoDuca’s signing responsibility, the March filing, later continued advocacy, May acknowledgement and June sanctions. It finds subjective bad faith and orders client and judge notices; payment and delivery are not established.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The court established fake opinions, continued reliance and sanctionable conduct. The represented later framework versions are excluded from the historical filings. Contemporary general AI validation and risk-documentation practices remain unresolved where their decisive records are unavailable. The court’s findings are not converted into a later AI-standard duty. The sanctions order also establishes an adverse professional credibility reaction to continued advocacy and actual court-work burden. Those consequences remain independent of the fine and of the retained class failures; hypothetical injuries to other parties do not determine the harm band. The submissions attributed generated opinions and quotations to courts and judges that had not supplied them. The sanctions order identifies falsely named judicial authors and fabricated source text. This false attribution is distinct from inadequate checking and reliance on the material as legal authority.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: Generative systems can produce fluent legal forms without the underlying authorities they purport to cite. In professional settings, users and organisations need source verification, traceable retrieval and effective challenge procedures before generated material is filed or used to affect another person's rights.
assessment_boundaries: The court's sanctions findings establish the conduct and penalty in this proceeding; the record does not determine broader professional discipline or liability.
The record does not infer which ChatGPT model version produced the material or the internal cause of the nonexistent citations.
The model output did not file itself; the lawyers' verification and submission decisions remain a material part of the occurrence.

The sanction, court-work burden and actual professional credibility findings are assessed separately. Potential injury to other judges, parties or legal-system trust is not treated as materialised. No AI-caused merits loss or dilatory delay is established.

taxonomy_classification.classification_basis: Generated nonexistent opinions and fake quotations entered formal court submissions that required substantially greater assurance of source existence and legal authority than generative drafting supplied. Counsel also failed to verify that the cited opinions existed and continued to stand by the material after authenticity was questioned. The court record therefore supports both misplaced reliance on generated legal material and a distinct omission of required verification. The submissions attributed generated opinions and quotations to courts and judges that had not supplied them. The sanctions order identifies falsely named judicial authors and fabricated source text. This false attribution is distinct from inadequate checking and reliance on the material as legal authority.

primary_classification.classification_basis: ChatGPT-generated nonexistent judicial opinions and fake quotations were incorporated into formal court submissions as usable legal authority despite failing the factual, source and legal-fidelity threshold required for judicial reliance.

secondary_classifications.classification_basis: Counsel relied on the generated authorities without verifying that the cited opinions existed before filing, directly establishing omission of a material verification step required for the reliance-bearing legal task.

harm_impact_assessment.coverage_note: All twelve dimensions source-reviewed. The court established bad faith in the individual lawyers’ continued advocacy, imposed sanctions and ordered notification to the client and falsely named judges. That adverse professional credibility finding supports reputation S3 independently of the US$5,000 financial sanction. The actual court search, hearing and corrective work support localised workflow S2. The order distinguishes potential injury to others and expressly does not find dilatory delay; neither changed merits nor detention is inferred. Relational-role and heightened personal-protection boundaries independently tested.

The court and opposing counsel searched for nonexistent authorities; show-cause proceedings, a hearing and corrective submissions followed. This is actual localised workflow burden addressed by the ordinary court process. The order expressly states delay and dilatory tactics were not the harms found. No whole-service outage, altered merits or maximum-tolerable-downtime breach is inferred.

The court individually found the lawyers acted in bad faith through conscious avoidance and misleading representations, sanctioned them and required client/judge notification. This is an observed adverse professional credibility reaction with bounded remedy, supporting S3 beyond embarrassment. Potential injury to the falsely named judges, fictional parties or public trust is not converted into realised harm without independent consequence evidence.
